cards.title: From {handCleaned} to 2,000,000
cards.body: You cleaned {handCleaned} records by hand. Data scientists write each rule once as code. A pipeline, an automatic chain of steps, then applies it to millions of records in seconds.

cards.title: Your labels did this
cards.body: Every picture you labelled helped train your model, the program that learnt from your examples. More good labels, more accurate guesses.

cards.title: Clear road: 91%?
cards.body: Your model says this road is clear, 91% sure. It's flooded. Your model never saw night photos. Real AI teams hunt for gaps like this and keep humans checking the results.

cards.title: Your blocks, as code
cards.body: Your blocks just turned into Python, a real programming language. Same logic, different words. Programming is breaking a problem into clear steps.

cards.title: Tested before it ships
cards.body: Software engineers also write automatic tests: small checks that run your program on thousands of maps before real people use it. Each tick is a passed test.

cards.title: Pods
cards.body: Pods: small identical copies of your app. Kubernetes, a tool that manages apps, runs many at once.

cards.title: Load balancer
cards.body: A load balancer spreads users evenly across your pods, so no single copy gets swamped.

cards.title: Autoscaler
cards.body: The autoscaler adds pods when it's busy and removes them when it's quiet, saving money.

cards.title: Self-healing
cards.body: Kubernetes checks each pod's health. If one crashes, it replaces it automatically. No more frantic tapping.

cards.title: Rolling updates
cards.body: New versions go out a few pods at a time. If checks fail, Kubernetes rolls back automatically.
Site reliability engineers (SREs) keep apps like this running for millions of people. They set up alerts so a human only gets woken up when automation can't fix it.
